title: Torn from behind
hook: the shirt is torn from the back, and a witness says that proves who ran

segments.voice: Yesterday: ma'adha-llah, the house of the Aziz, and a young man who ran to refuge. Your line was I seek refuge. Did you turn toward it once when something knocked? Day sixty-one.

Yusuf said I seek refuge in Allah, and then he did the most practical thing a person can do with temptation. He ran for the door. She ran after him. They both raced for it, the Qur'an says, and she caught hold of his shirt from behind, and it tore. And then the door opens, and there, standing in the doorway, is her husband. Everyone freezes. It's a moment straight out of a courtroom drama, except there's no courtroom and no lawyer. Just two stories, one husband, and a torn shirt. Today: torn from behind.
screen: `HE RUNS FOR THE DOOR.` → `SHE CATCHES HIS SHIRT.` → `THE HUSBAND IN THE DOORWAY.`

segments.voice: Surah Yusuf. She speaks first, fast. What's the penalty for someone who meant harm to your wife, except prison or a painful punishment? She doesn't even say what he did. She jumps to the sentence. Yusuf answers simply: she tried to turn me from myself. That's all. And then a witness from her own family speaks. The Qur'an says only a witness of her household; who it was, the text doesn't say. Some commentators report it was a wise man of her family; others tell a story that it was an infant who spoke. The witness says: look at the shirt. If it's torn from the front, she's telling the truth and he's lying. If it's torn from the back, she's lying and he's telling the truth. It's simple, almost like a detective's rule. Someone lunging at you tears the front. Someone running from you gets caught from behind. The husband looks. Torn from behind. And he says: this is your scheming, and turns to Yusuf: leave this alone. And to his wife: ask forgiveness for your wrong. Notice what Yusuf did not do. He didn't give a speech. He didn't attack her. He said one true sentence and let the evidence speak. And this is the second shirt in the surah. The first came home with false blood on it, and it lied. This one is torn from behind, and it tells the truth. There's one more shirt still to come in this story. Keep an eye on the shirts.
screen: `HER STORY COMES FIRST.` · `ONE TRUE SENTENCE.` · `A WITNESS: LOOK AT THE SHIRT.` · `THE SECOND SHIRT TELLS THE TRUTH.` · then, large: `TORN FROM BEHIND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let the truth speak for itself once. Settle, and breathe. Think of a situation where you feel misunderstood, or accused, or where someone has the story wrong. Notice how much you want to explain, defend, send the long message, win. Now imagine saying one true, calm sentence, and stopping there. Just one. Let the facts, the shirt, do the rest. Say the sentence to yourself a few times, and feel what it's like not to add more. If you pray, you can ask for the truth to come out in its own time. The bell holds the time.
Qamis, shirt: the one torn from behind, that showed who ran and who chased, and let Yusuf stop after one true sentence.
Your line: the shirt tells. The next time you're tempted to over-explain today, say the one true sentence, and let it stand. Day sixty-one.

screen: `DAY 61 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE KNIVES AND THE FRUIT.`

howItsDone: Muslims often point to the torn shirt as an example of Allah bringing the truth to light, and to Yusuf's calm answer as the way to respond when falsely accused.

fork.reveal: if the shirt is torn in front, she's truthful; if behind, he is. it was torn from behind.

original.note: Arabic: shirt — a word that carries Surah Yusuf from one turn to the next.

trapdoor: what you thought: a he-said, she-said.
what it means: Yusuf says one true sentence, and the evidence, a shirt torn from behind, tells the rest.
what a scholar hears: qamis, the shirt, marks three turns in Surah Yusuf: false blood (12:18), torn from behind (12:26–28), and the shirt that restores Ya'qub's sight (12:93–96).

notes: The witness: the Qur'an says 'a witness of her own folk'. Commentators give different identities, including a man of her family and (in some reports) an infant who spoke. Both are mentioned as commentary. Confirm the Keeper wants the infant report mentioned.
Who says 'this is your scheming' (12:28) and addresses Yusuf and the wife (12:29): usually taken as the husband; some read 12:29 as the witness. Script follows the usual reading.
The trapdoor names the third shirt (12:93–96) ahead of its day as a scholar's note; the teach only says 'one more shirt still to come'.
